Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the trigger set is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and with the rest of the profile. Motorcycle noise, ambulances, and hospital/antiseptic smells together suggest an injury/medical-emergency aftermath pattern rather than a primary disaster-linked cue pattern. A disaster survivor could have some of these cues, but all three together without any disaster-specific trigger makes the trigger node clinically questionable.

'Guilt on recall' is not impossible after a natural disaster, but in this profile it lacks support from any negative appraisal items and sits awkwardly alongside a formulation where Memory is strongly linked to Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies but not to Negative Appraisals or Threat. The selected memory items otherwise describe sensory reliving and fragmented snapshots; adding intense guilt introduces a meaning-based response not reflected elsewhere.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: 'Wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed' is difficult to connect to the listed triggers and memory items for a natural disaster survivor. It implies fears about being seen, targeted, or scrutinized, which are not represented in the trigger or memory content and are not supported by active edges involving threat or negative appraisals.

issues.item: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, 'wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed' is hard to reconcile with the presented trigger pattern and memory content. This strategy implies interpersonal scrutiny or targeted threat, but the profile contains no corresponding threat/appraisal items and the trauma type is non-interpersonal.

issues.item: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' is weakly grounded in the rest of the profile. The triggers are external reminder cues and the memory items emphasize sensory reliving/snapshot recall, but there is no corresponding bodily injury theme, threat belief, or appraisal that would make persistent body checking a coherent central strategy.

issues.item: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: 'When I remember the event I feel intense guilt' is not impossible after a natural disaster, but in this profile it lacks support from any negative appraisal content and does not fit the otherwise cue-driven sensory reliving formulation. It stands out as an unsupported meaning-based reaction within a profile whose active edges are concentrated around triggers, memory, and maladaptive strategies rather than appraisals.

issues.item: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: This item is not clinically well aligned with the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. The triggers and memory items consistently describe sensory re-experiencing of a disaster, and the formulation strongly links Triggers ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies. 'Concealing clothing to avoid being noticed' implies an interpersonal scrutiny or targeted-harm concern that is not supported by the listed triggers, memory content, or any threat/appraisal items. It addresses a different problem type than the rest of the profile and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation.

vignette:
Arun Sothy was 31 when he came for treatment, a married Cambodian American man serving as a judge in a busy county court. He described the disaster in fragments that arrived as pictures more than words, and even in session he tended to speak around it at first, as if saying too much might pull him back into it. The event had happened during severe storm conditions while he was visiting family in a coastal area. He remembered the day less as a sequence than as a set of frozen images: the sky turning an odd color, rain driven sideways, water rising where it should not have been, the sudden confusion of people shouting over wind and sirens. What remained with him most strongly were a few visual moments that seemed cut out of time-standing in floodwater that had climbed too fast, seeing emergency vehicles trying to reach stranded residents, and the bright, clinical interior of a hospital area where survivors were being assessed after the storm. Even now, when the memory returned, it did not feel like recollection. He said it came back "all at once," as if he were there again, with the sights, sounds, bodily sensations, and smell of antiseptic becoming completely real for a moment.

In the weeks afterward, Arun tried to carry on with the discipline that had always defined him. He returned to work, put on his robe, heard cases, and told himself to stay focused on facts and procedure. He was determined not to think about the disaster. If an image began to intrude-a flash of dark water, emergency lights reflecting on wet pavement, the sharp hospital smell-he would force his attention elsewhere, press forward with the next task, and speak even more precisely from the bench. From the outside he appeared controlled. Internally, he was working constantly to push the pictures back down.

Certain moments in daily life quickly became charged. Ambulance sirens were especially difficult. In his courthouse, emergency vehicles regularly passed the building on the street below, and the sound could cut through proceedings without warning. When that happened, Arun felt his body tense before he had time to think. The courtroom around him could seem to drop away and be replaced by those storm scenes: flashing lights through heavy rain, urgency, people trying to get somewhere impossible to reach. He also became acutely aware of smell. Passing near the courthouse clinic, accompanying someone to a hospital, or catching the clean chemical scent of antiseptic on a hallway or elevator triggered an immediate sense that the disaster was present again. He did not experience these as memories in the ordinary sense. They were vivid, sensory episodes, dominated by images, as if the mind had stored the event in pictures and then projected them straight back into the room.

Weather was another problem. On days when the air felt like it had before the disaster-thick, storm-heavy, with the particular dimness that comes before severe rain-Arun became watchful and restless. He found it hard to settle at home, hard to sit on the couch with his wife, hard to do anything that resembled letting his guard down. He had come to feel that relaxation itself was unsafe. If he loosened his attention, something terrible could happen again and catch him unprepared. So even in quiet evenings he remained mentally braced, checking forecasts, looking out the window, staying upright when his wife urged him to rest.

Over time, he also began limiting how much he went out. He kept his routines narrow: home, court, essential errands only. He declined social invitations and cut short family outings, especially when bad weather threatened or if the destination involved hospitals or dense downtown traffic where ambulances were common. He told himself he was being practical, but the pattern gradually shrank his life. His wife noticed that he seemed absent even when physically present, always managing his surroundings, always ready to leave. At work, the strain showed in quieter ways. He still performed competently, but colleagues saw him becoming more rigid about breaks and less willing to step into informal conversations in the hallway if sirens or commotion outside might interrupt.

By the time Arun sought help, he was exhausted by the effort of holding the disaster out of mind. What finally pushed him to come was a recent storm warning during a court day: thunder rolled outside, an ambulance passed, and for a few seconds he was no longer in his courtroom but back inside those visual snapshots, with the smell and panic so real that he had to pause the proceedings. He was ashamed that this had happened in public, but what frightened him more was how fully real it had felt. He said he wanted help because he could no longer keep living "on alert" every day. At the same time, he was afraid that if he stopped suppressing the memories, they would overtake him completely. What he hoped for, carefully stated, was not to erase what happened but to be able to hear a siren, smell a hospital corridor, or watch storm clouds gather without feeling as though the disaster had returned.
